rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage resumes after describing Muhammad’s mission and signals the hoped-for future outcome, completing this account’s beginning and end in parallel with earlier prophetic stories.
rows.anchor: استئناف ابتدائي بعدما مضى من وصف رسالة محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم وإجمال أصلها وأمره بإنذارهم وتسجيل التبليغ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to seek God’s judgment and help after the warning that they will turn away implies their certain rejection and God’s just requital.
rows.anchor: وفي أمر الله تعالى نبيئه عليه الصلاة والسلام بالالتجاء إليه والاستعانة به بعدما قال له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When God teaches servants a supplication, He guarantees its answer; Ibn ʿĀshūr compares the taught prayer in al-Baqara.
rows.anchor: لأن الله إذا لقن عباده دعاء فقد ضمن لهم إجابته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God fulfilled this promise and answered His servant by judging the defiant opponents at Badr.
rows.anchor: وقد صدق الله وعده واستجاب لعبده فحكم في هؤلاء المعاندين بالحق يوم بدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is to say this within their hearing as a challenge, entrusting God to judge them by truth that will break their power and invalidate their religion.
rows.anchor: قل ذلك بمسمع منهم إظهارا لتحديه إياهم بأنه فوض أمره إلى ربه ليحكم فيهم بالحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prefixed bāʾ in “with truth” denotes الملابسة, accompaniment or connection.
rows.anchor: الباء في قوله تعالى { بالحق } للملابسة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted second complement of “judge” signals that the Prophet is on the truth: he asks God to judge for him, against them, or between them.
rows.anchor: وحذف المتعلق الثاني لفعل { احكم } لتنبيههم إلى أن النبي على الحق فإنه ما سأل الحكم بالحق إلا لأنه يريده

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most reciters read قل as an imperative; Ḥafṣ reads قال in the past tense, as in the verse near the beginning of this surah.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور { قل } بصيغة الأمر . وقرأ حفص { قال } بصيغة الماضي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The past-tense reading is a report of the Prophet’s words, though the Kufan codex does not write the alif.
rows.anchor: ولم يكتب في المصحف الكوفي بإثبات الألف . على أنه حكاية عن الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the vocative Rabb, the first-person possessive yāʾ is omitted, with the kasra left as its sign.
rows.anchor: و { رب } منادى مضاف حذفت منه ياء المتكلم المضاف هو إليها وبقيت الكسرة دليلا على الياء

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most reciters pronounce the bāʾ of Rabb with kasra; Abū Jaʿfar uses ḍamma, an Arabic vocative form akin to apocope when ambiguity is avoided.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور بكسر الباء من { رب . وقرأه أبو جعفر بضم الباء وهو وجه عربي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The possessive in “our Lord” honors Muslims by affirming their connection to God as their Lord.
rows.anchor: لتضمنها تعظيما لشأن المسلمين بالاعتزاز بأن الله ربهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first-person plural includes the Prophet and Muslims, while indirectly suggesting idolaters have no share in God’s lordship because they worship idols; Ibn ʿĀshūr links this to Muḥammad 47:11.
rows.anchor: وضمير المتكلم المشارك للنبيء ومن معه من المسلمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḥmān is an appositive clarifying Rabb, used as the divine name to taunt idolaters who rejected that name.
rows.anchor: والرحمان عطف بيان من { ربنا } لأن المراد به هنا الاسم لا الوصف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite form of al-mustaʿān conveys restriction: help is sought from God alone, as in “You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help.”
rows.anchor: وتعريف { المستعان } لإفادة القصر ، أي لا أستعين بغيره على ما تصفون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After “against what you describe,” an object is omitted: God is asked to help invalidate their claims and expose them so people do not follow them, or to stop their harm and incitement against the Prophet and believers.
rows.anchor: على إبطال ما تصفون بإظهار بطلانكم للناس حتى يؤمنوا ولا يتبعوكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “What you describe” means their abusive statements: they called the Prophet mad and a sorcerer and called the Qurʾān poetry and tales of the ancients, publicizing this to incite people.
rows.anchor: وهم وصفوا النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بصفات ذم كقولهم : مجنون وساحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is coordinated with the preceding statement that the offerings reach the Ancient House.
rows.anchor: عطف على جملة { ثم محلها إلى البيت العتيق } ( الحج : 33 )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Community” means people sharing a religion; Muslims’ single ritual site is the Ancient House.
rows.anchor: أهل الدين الذين اشتركوا في اتباعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement rebuts idolaters who devised rites, times, and slaughter sites for their idols, such as al-Ghabghab, the slaughter place of al-ʿUzzā.
rows.anchor: والمقصود من هذا الرد على المشركين إذ جعلوا لأصنامهم مناسك تشابه مناسك الحج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gave each community one place for sacrifice to Him, the provider of the livestock; an idol that neither creates nor provides the animals deserves no sacrificial rite, so the rites are not multiple.
rows.anchor: فذكرهم الله تعالى بأنه ما جعل لكل أمة إلا منسكا واحدا للقربان إلى الله تعالى الذي رزق الناس الأنعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite mansakan means one, not several; the emphasis falls on God as the one who established it.
rows.anchor: فالتنكير في قوله { منسكا } للإفراد ، أي واحدا لا متعددا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The following remembrance of God’s name and explicit statement that the deity is one reinforce the interpretation; the wording also invites Muslims to follow other communities of true religion.
rows.anchor: والكلام يفيد الاقتداء ببقية الأمم أهل الأديان الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On one reading, ʿalā is figuratively “upon,” attached to remembering God’s name with an omitted noun: at offering the provision, by slaughtering it.
rows.anchor: { على } يجوز أن تكون للاستعلاء المجازي متعلقة ب { يذكروا اسم الله }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, ʿalā means “for,” so God’s name is remembered because of the livestock He provided.
rows.anchor: ليذكروا اسم الله لأجل ما رزقهم من بهيمة الأنعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oneness of the sanctuary points to one deity, since many deities would have differing laws; the fronted “to Him” restricts submission to God alone and rejects rites for idols.
rows.anchor: أي إذ كان قد جعل لكم منسكا واحدا فقد نبهكم بذلك أنه إله واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause ordering is shifted: its underlying order is “submit to God, because your deity is one”; the fronting of “to Him” restricts submission.
rows.anchor: وأصل النظم : فلله أسلموا ، لأن إلهكم إله واحد . وتقديم المجرور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Submitting means complete obedience and sincere worship: abandon every rite established for other than God and perform only the rite He established.
rows.anchor: والإسلام : الانقياد التام ، وهو الإخلاص في الطاعة

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most reciters read mansakan with fatḥa on the sīn; Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Khalaf read it with kasra. Both readings are a place noun for ritual sacrifice.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور { منسكا } بفتح السين وقرأه حمزة ، والكسائي ، وخلف بكسر السين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fatḥa follows the regular pattern for a place noun from nasaka yansuku; the kasra is an attested exception, like masjid from sajada yasjudu.
rows.anchor: إلا أنه على قراءة الجمهور جار على القياس لأن قياسه الفتح في اسم المكان إذ هو من نسك ينسك بضم العين في المضارع

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī says al-Kisāʾī may have heard the kasra form from Arabs.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي الفارسي : ويشبه أن الكسائي سمعه من العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to give good news interrupts the list of blessings; the Prophet is addressed, and the described people are Muslims.
rows.anchor: والخطاب للنبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم وأصحاب هذه الصفات هم المسلمون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mukhbit means humble and free of arrogance; its root evokes entering a low tract of land, metaphorically lowering oneself.
rows.anchor: والمخبت : المتواضع الذي لا تكبر عنده . وأصل المخبت من سلك الخبت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers’ humility contrasts with the arrogance of idolaters, as also stated in Ghāfir.
rows.anchor: لأن التواضع من شيمهم كما كان التكبر من سمات المشركين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wajal is intense fear; Ibn ʿĀshūr points to its earlier use in the account of Abraham’s guests.
rows.anchor: والوجل : الخوف الشديد . وتقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The four qualities are fear at God’s mention, patience under harm for His sake, prayer, and spending; they express humility and are required when practicable, not when a believer lacks resources.
rows.anchor: وكل هذه الصفات الأربع مظاهر للتواضع فليس المقصود من جمع تلك الصفات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The intended spending is for needy, vulnerable believers; hospitality to guests and friends was also a practice of boastful Arabs, as Ibn ʿĀshūr noted at al-Baqara 2:180.
rows.anchor: والمراد من الإنفاق الإنفاق على المحتاجين الضعفاء من المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr compares spending on convivial drinking and completing wagers, citing al-Nābigha.
rows.anchor: وهو نظير الإنفاق على الندماء في مجالس الشراب . ونظير إتمام الإيسار في مواقع الميسر ، كما قال النابغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse coordinates with the rule for ritual sacrifice, making the camels designated as offerings among God’s sacred signs.
rows.anchor: عطف على جملة { ولكل أمة جعلنا منسكا } ( الحج : 34 ) أي جعلنا منسكا للقربان والهدايا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God commanded camel offerings at Hajj from Abraham’s time, as compensation for concessions in Hajj and as voluntary offerings bearing promised reward; this divine designation gives them blessing and sanctity.
rows.anchor: والمعنى : أن الله أمر بقربان البدن في الحج من عهد إبراهيم عليه السلام وجعلها جزاء عما يترخص فيه من أعمال الحج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Badana denotes a large-bodied camel, from the sense of bulk and fatness; its plural is badan, with the usual ḍamma on dāl commonly lightened to sukūn, and the term came to mean a camel designated for offering.
rows.anchor: والبدن : جمع بدنة بالتحريك ، وهي البعير العظيم البدن . وهو اسم مأخوذ من البدانة

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet repeatedly told a man leading a hady camel to ride it despite the man’s objection that it was a badana; this identifies the badana as a Hajj offering.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم رأى رجلا يسوق بدنة فقال : اركبها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word al-budn is fronted before its governing verb to emphasize its importance.
rows.anchor: وتقديم { البدن } على عامله للاهتمام بها تنويها بشأنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Camels are singled out as the best Hajj offerings because of their abundant meat; Sunna extends the category to cattle and sheep, collectively called hady.
rows.anchor: والاقتصار على البدن الخاصص بالإبل لأنها أفضل في الهدي لكثرة لحمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the animals God’s signs means He made them markers of Hajj and sacred; this explains the practice of marking an offering camel’s skin, called ishʿār.
rows.anchor: ومعنى كونها من شعائر الله : أن الله جعلها معالم تؤذن بالحج وجعل لها حرمة

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: In the Muwaṭṭaʾ, Mālik reports that ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar garlanded and marked offerings at Dhū al-Ḥulayfa, garlanding them first and marking the left side of the hump before slaughter.
rows.anchor: قال مالك في ( الموطأ ) : ( كان عبد الله بن عمر إذا أهدى هديا من المدينة قلده وأشعره بذي الحليفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to eat from the offering could mean obligation, permission, or recommendation; obligation is unlikely because natural appetite already prompts eating. The verse instead removes the pre-Islamic ban, leaving permission or recommendation open.
rows.anchor: والأمر في قوله { فكلوا منها } مجمل ، يحتمل الوجوب ويحتمل الإباحة ويحتمل الندب

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik permits and recommends eating from obligatory offerings, except the expiation for injury, game penalty, and vow for the poor; he relies on the verse’s general wording subject to those exceptions.
rows.anchor: فقال مالك : يباح الأكل من لحوم الهدايا الواجبة ، وهو عنده مستحب

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa permits eating from tamattuʿ and qirān offerings, but not an obligatory offering designated by the pilgrim at consecration.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حنيفة : يأكل من هدي التمتع والقران ، ولا يأكل من الواجب

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī prohibits eating any offering, reasoning by analogy that a pilgrim who must give the offering from his property cannot then eat from it; Ibn al-ʿArabī reports this argument.
rows.anchor: وقال الشافعي : لا يأكل من لحوم الهدايا بحالل مستندا إلى القياس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr says that if this is the full extent of al-Shāfiʿī’s argument, it is weak: the Qurʾānic wording opposes it, and sound reports establish that the Prophet and Companions ate offerings.
rows.anchor: وإذا كان هذا قصارى كلام الشافعي فهو استدلال غير وجيه ولفظ القرآن ينافيه لا سيما وقد ثبت أكل النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وأصحابه من لحوم الهدايا بأحاديث صحيحة

rows.speaker: أحمد
rows.claim: Aḥmad permits eating from obligatory offerings except the game penalty and vow.
rows.anchor: وقال أحمد : يؤكل من الهدايا الواجبة إلا جزاء الصيد والنذر

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī holds that feeding the needy and the one who comes seeking is obligatory; Ibn al-ʿArabī says this is Mālik’s explicit position too.
rows.anchor: وأما الأمر في قوله : { وأطعموا القانع والمعتر } فقال الشافعي : للوجوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr says Mālik’s known view is that a person who only slaughters the offering without distributing from it is not sinful.
rows.anchor: وقلت : المعروف من قول مالك أنه لو اقتصر المهدي على نحر هديه ولم يتصدق منه ما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qāni is linked to qunūʿ, asking humbly; qanāʿa, contentment, has a different verbal pattern.
rows.anchor: والقانع : المتصف بالقنوع ، وهو التذلل

rows.speaker: الخفاجي
rows.claim: Al-Khafājī’s verse plays on the verbal distinction and praises contentment while condemning greed.
rows.anchor: ما أنشده الخفاجي : العبد حر إن قنع والحر عبد إن قنع فاقنع ولا تقنع فما شيء يشين سوى الطمع

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: In his Maqāmāt, al-Zamakhsharī advises Abū al-Qāsim to take contentment from qanāʿa rather than begging, and thus need neither giver nor denier.
rows.anchor: وللزمخشري في ( مقاماته ) : ( يا أبا القاسم اقنع من القناعة لا من القنوع

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: In the Muwaṭṭaʾ’s Book of Game, Mālik says the qāni is a poor person.
rows.anchor: وفي ( الموطأ ) في كتاب الصيد قال مالك : ( والقانع هو الفقير )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muʿtarr is an active participle meaning one who presents himself to receive a gift indirectly, by appearing where distribution occurs rather than asking.
rows.anchor: والمعتر : اسم فاعل من اعتر ، إذا تعرض للعطاء ، أي دون سؤال بل بالتعريض

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik reports hearing that muʿtarr means a visitor, from ʿarā, “to visit”; here the visit is to present oneself for a gift.
rows.anchor: وفي ( الموطأ ) في كتاب الصيد قال مالك : ( وسمعت أن المعتر هو الزائر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers the sense of a person presenting himself for a gift: coordination with qāni indicates distinct meanings, unlike bāʾis and faqīr in 22:28.
rows.anchor: فدل العطف على المغايرة ، ولو كانا في معنى واحد لما عطف عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Thus We subjected them to you” is a fresh expression of gratitude for creatures created to benefit people.
rows.anchor: وجملة { وكذلك سخرناها لكم } استئناف للامتنان بما خلق من المخلوقات لنفع الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their subjection is shown by strong livestock following one man and enduring marking and stabbing; without God’s implanted docility they would flee like wild animals weaker than them.
rows.anchor: والأمارة الدالة على إرادته ذلك أنه سخرها للناس مع ضعف الإنسان وقوة تلك الأنعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Likewise” refers to the extraordinary subjection people witness: God made the animals subject to them in the same manner.
rows.anchor: وقوله { كذلك } هو مثل نظائره ، أي مثل ذلك التسخير العجيب الذي ترونه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God created the animals subject to people to elicit gratitude through worship of Him alone, indirectly rebuking idolaters for misdirected gratitude.
rows.anchor: ومعنى { لعلكم تشكرون } خلقناها مسخرة لكم استجلابا لأن تشكروا الله بإفراده بالعبادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The consecutive faʾ indicates that Pharaoh and his elite did not consider the invitation, signs, or proof; instead, they were intensely arrogant, with the sīn and tāʾ reinforcing the intensity.
rows.anchor: وعطف { فاستكبروا } بفاء التعقيب يفيد أنهم لم يتأملوا الدعوة والآيات والحجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “They were an overbearing people” is an interrupting circumstantial clause about Pharaoh and his elite, explaining that their habitual pride drove them to reject Moses and Aaron.
rows.anchor: وجملة { وكانوا قوما عالين } معترضة بين فعل { استكبروا }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An attributive description attached to qawm indicates that the trait is ingrained in the people; here ʿuluww means arrogance and tyranny, to be explained at al-Qaṣaṣ 28:4.
rows.anchor: فالمعنى هنا : أن استكبارهم على تلقي دعوة موسى وآياته وحجته إنما نشأ عن سجيتهم من الكبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim about believing in two humans explains their arrogance; it was spoken by some members of the elite to one another, then attributed to all because they had agreed on it.
rows.anchor: وهذا ليس من قول فرعون ولكنه قول بعض الملإ لبعض ، ولما كانوا قد تراوضوا عليه نسب إليهم جميعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh listened to their counsel but had a separate declaration, that he knew no deity for them but himself; Ibn ʿĀshūr says he was treated as a deity, though human in appearance, as a son of gods.
rows.anchor: وأما فرعون فكان مصغيا لرأيهم ومشورتهم وكان له قول آخر حكي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their question is a denial: they deemed themselves unable to believe in two humans like them, since the messengers refuted the divinity of the idols they served.
rows.anchor: والاستفهام في { أنؤمن } إنكاري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Misguided elites demanded that a messenger differ in kind from those addressed, imagining hybrid bodily forms for their gods while ignoring the greater distinctions of soul and intellect; this fallacy led many nations to reject messengers.
rows.anchor: فكان ملأ فرعون لضلالهم يتطلبون لصحة الرسالة عن الله أن يكون الرسول مباينا للمرسل إليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām after āman is transitive when someone is believed because of trust in the speaker; its original force is causal, as in the examples from al-ʿAnkabūt and al-Dukhān.
rows.anchor: واللام في قوله : { لبشرين } لتعدية فعل { نؤمن } . يقال للذي يصدق المخبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Āmantu bi-Muḥammad means believing the content or message, while āmantu li-Muḥammad means trusting Muhammad about what he brought; one says āman bi-Allāh, not āman li-Allāh.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الأول يتعلق بذاته وهو الرسالة ومعنى الثاني أنك صدقته فيما جاء به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mithlana may remain masculine singular despite its dual feminine noun, or agree with its noun, as in al-Aʿrāf 7:194.
rows.anchor: دون نظر إلى مخالفة صيغه موصوفه كما هنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After attacking the messengers’ humanity, the elites attack their origins: their people are allegedly servants of the elites and thus inferior, so the messengers should not rule them.
rows.anchor: وهذا طعن في رسالتهما من جانب حالهما الذاتي ثم أعقبوه بطعن من جهة منشئهما وقبيلهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿĀbidūn means obedient and submissive; the Israelites had been servants and laborers for the Copts, as in al-Shuʿarāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقوله : { عابدون } جمع عابد ، أي مطيع خاضع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The elite’s settled decision was to reject the two messengers; their rejection led to their drowning and inclusion among the destroyed peoples, a more forceful formulation than simply saying they were destroyed.
rows.anchor: أي أرسى أمرهم على أن كذبوهما ، ثم فرع على تكذيبهم أن كانوا من المهلكين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence is customary rather than instantaneous: their rejection persisted until the drowning that resulted from it.
rows.anchor: والتعقيب هنا تعقيب عرفي لأن الإغراق لما نشأ عن التكذيب فالتكذيب مستمر إلى حين الإهلاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling them “among the destroyed” warns Quraysh that God’s established pattern is to destroy those who reject His messengers.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا تعريض بتهديد قريش على تكذيبهم رسولهم صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s curse means worldly consequences—being treated as sinful, losing eligibility to testify, alienation from believers, and the prescribed slander penalty—and, in the afterlife, exclusion from mercy.
rows.anchor: واللعن : في الدنيا التفسيق ، وسلب أهلية الشهادة ، واستيحاش المؤمنين منهم ، وحد القذف ، واللعن في الآخرة : الإبعاد من رحمة الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “day their tongues testify” clause modifies the time attached to their great punishment; bodily testimony is mentioned to terrify them into repentance.
rows.anchor: وذكر شهادة ألسنتهم وأيديهم وأرجلهم للتهويل عليهم لعلهم يتقون ذلك الموقف فيتوبون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The testimony of body parts against their owners is one of the states in the reckoning of disbelievers.
rows.anchor: وشهادة الأعضاء على صاحبها من أحوال حساب الكفار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These particular limbs are named because they took part in slander: tongues uttered it, hands pointed at the accused, and feet carried it to public gatherings; the whole body may testify, as in Fuṣṣilat.
rows.anchor: لأن لهذه الأعضاء عملا في رمي المحصنات فهم ينطقون بالقذف ويشيرون بالأيدي إلى المقذوفات ويسعون بأرجلهم إلى مجالس الناس لإبلاغ القذف

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي وخلف
rows.claim: Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Khalaf read yashhadu in the masculine singular, a valid agreement pattern for a verb with a broken-plural subject.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي وخلف { يشهد عليهم } بالتحتية ، وذلك وجه في الفعل المسند إلى ضمير جمع تكسير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that God will repay them answers the question raised by the limbs’ testimony: He recompenses them for what those limbs have testified; dīn means recompense, as in al-Fātiḥa.
rows.anchor: لأن ذكر شهادة الأعضاء يثير سؤالا عن آثار تلك الشهادة فيجاب بأن أثرها أن يجازيهم الله على ما شهدت به أعضاؤهم عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥaqq modifies dīn, meaning a just recompense without injustice; a verbal noun is used adjectivally for emphasis.
rows.anchor: و { الحق } نعت للدين ، أي الجزاء العادل الذي لا ظلم فيه فوصف بالمصدر للمبالغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The truth of God becomes manifest to people; al-ḥaqq as a verbal noun can mean the necessarily existing, whose being is never preceded by or open to nonexistence.
rows.anchor: ووصف الله بأنه { الحق } وصف بالمصدر لإفادة تحقق اتصافه بالحق

rows.speaker: الغزالي
rows.claim: Al-Ghazālī, in his commentary on the divine names, limits the meaning of God’s name al-Ḥaqq to necessary, unchanging existence.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا المعنى في اسمه تعالى : { الحق } اقتصر الغزالي في ( شرح الأسماء الحسنى )

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: The alternative sense of al-ḥaqq is the possessor of justice, fitting its placement after “their just recompense”; al-Zamakhsharī gives this interpretation in al-Kashshāf.
rows.anchor: وثانيهما : معنى أنه ذو الحق ، أي العدل وهو الذي يناسب وقوع الوصف بعد قوله : { دينهم الحق }

rows.speaker: ابن برجان الإشبيلي
rows.claim: Ibn Barjān, al-Qurṭubī, and possibly al-Zamakhsharī treat al-Ḥaqq as God’s name, while al-Zamakhsharī may only be explaining the word’s sense here.
rows.anchor: وهذا الذي درج عليه ابن برجان الإشبيلي في كتابه ( شرح الأسماء الحسنى ) والقرطبي في ( التفسير )

rows.speaker: الخنساء
rows.claim: Al-Khansāʾ’s cited line uses the verbal nouns iqbāl and idbār as predicate, illustrating the verbal noun used to convey a firmly realized quality.
rows.anchor: كقول الخنساء : ترتع ما رتعت حتى إذا ادكرت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥaqq is among God’s beautiful names. Al-mubīn can modify al-ḥaqq as “clear truth,” or modify God as “the one who makes clear and guides”; al-Qurṭubī and Ibn Barjān list al-Mubīn as a divine name.
rows.anchor: ولك أن تجعله وصفا لله تعالى بمعنى أن الله مبين وهاد
